title: Repaint the signposts until none change
allegory: Policy iteration is improving a park's signposts: walk the park following the current signs and write down what each square is worth, then repaint every sign toward its best-looking neighbour, and repeat until no sign wants repainting.
map: a signpost on every square of the park
the policy π: one action per state, an integer array
walking the park by the signs, tallying what each square is worth
policy evaluation: V_π(s) for every state
repainting each sign toward the best-looking next square
policy improvement: π′(s) = argmaxₐ Σ T·(R + γV_π)
the policy is stable, and therefore optimal
a coin toss between two equally good signs, every round
random tie-breaking: equally optimal policies swap forever

chapters.name: A park of signposts
chapters.note: are these the best signs? how would I fix them?

cap.1: You have the full map of a small park: every square, every move, every reward. Each square has a signpost. Are these the best signs? How would you fix them?
cap.2: In [2.1] the gridworld's dynamics come as arrays, T[s, a, s′] and R[s, a, s′]. A deterministic policy is just an integer array: one action per state.
cap.3: Tabular planning in a known MDP: T and R given, π deterministic. Goal: an optimal policy, found by alternating exact evaluation with greedy improvement (Howard, 1960).

cap.1: First walk the park by the signs and write down what each square is worth. Then repaint every sign toward the best-looking neighbour. Repeat.
cap.2: Evaluate the current policy (its value in every state), then improve it by choosing, in each state, the action with the best one-step lookahead. Alternate until nothing changes.
cap.3: Policy iteration: compute V_π from the Bellman expectation equation, set π′ = greedy(V_π), repeat. The policy improvement theorem gives V_π′ ≥ V_π in every state.

parts.note: point the sign at the winner

cap.1: At each square, try every direction in your head: the reward for the step, plus what the landing square is worth. Point the sign at the winner.
cap.2: Improvement is one line: per state, the action maximising expected reward plus γ × the next state's value, using the V you just computed. np.argmax does it per state.
cap.3: π′(s) = argmaxₐ Σₛ′ T(s′|s,a)[R(s,a,s′) + γV_π(s′)], greedy w.r.t. Q_π. Evaluation can be exact: V_π = (I − γP_π)⁻¹ r_π, one linear solve.

chapters.name: Good news spreads
chapters.title: toy grid: all signs began ←; lit in the order repainted

cap.1: All signs start pointing left. Each round, good news spreads one square further back from the goal and those signs get repainted. After five rounds: no change.
cap.2: On this toy grid (step cost −0.04, γ = 0.9), rounds repaint 1, 2, 2, 2, then 1 signs, then none. The start square's value rises from −0.40 to 0.49.
cap.3: From π₀ = all-left, each greedy step extends the goal-reaching path by one state; round 6 changes nothing, so π is optimal. The bottom-right ← correctly avoids the −1.

chapters.name: The endless flip
chapters.verdict: Break ties deterministically; compare whole policy arrays.

cap.1: On our grid, going up or right from the start is exactly as good. Toss a coin each round and that sign keeps flipping, so the plan never 'stops changing'.
cap.2: Ties in the argmax can make two optimal policies swap forever. Break ties deterministically (np.argmax takes the first) and stop when (pi_new == pi_old).all(). Keep γ < 1.
cap.3: Termination needs strict improvement or exact repetition; stochastic tie-breaking cycles among equally optimal policies. With γ = 1 the update is no contraction and I − γP_π can be singular.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Evaluate, then improve: the RL skeleton
SARSA, Q-learning, DQN: same loop, no map
Actor-critic and RLHF keep the rhythm

cap.1: Nearly every RL method you will meet is this loop with the map taken away: judge the plan, nudge it towards better, repeat.
cap.2: SARSA, Q-learning and DQN swap the known T and R for samples but keep the rhythm: estimate values, then act more greedily on them. Policy iteration is the clean version.
cap.3: Actor-critic methods, including the PPO used in RLHF to steer language models, keep the evaluate-improve rhythm; the exact loop shows what their approximations give up.

coda.title: Set the signposts: each tap turns a sign a quarter-turn clockwise

readouts.label: squares where a strictly better sign exists

caption.1: Every sign starts pointing left. Tap squares to turn their signs. Watch the start square's value climb, and keep going until no square can do better.
caption.2: Readouts evaluate your signs (γ = 0.9, step −0.04, 80 sweeps) and run the improvement check: squares with a strictly better sign. None left means optimal. +1, −1 and ■ ignore taps.
caption.3: Iterative policy evaluation plus a greedy check with strict improvement, so ties count as stable: the same rule that stops the real loop flip-flopping. Optimal V(start) here is 0.492.

where_else: SARSA and Q-learning: the same loop, with sampled experience instead of a known map
Actor-critic methods, including the PPO used in RLHF: a critic evaluates, the actor improves
k-means clustering: assign, re-centre, repeat until nothing changes

hamming.what: Alternating two steps, scoring the current plan in every state and then switching each state to its best-looking action, until the plan stops changing.
hamming.when: Whenever you know the full rules of a small world (transition and reward tables), as in the [2.1] gridworld exercises.
hamming.why: Each round can only help and there are finitely many plans, so it must stop, and it stops at an optimal one; later RL methods are this loop with the map removed.

object.title: The rising park
object.subtitle: Each square's tower is its value under the current signs; turn the knob to run the rounds and watch value flow back from the goal.

cap.1: All signs point left, so every square just bumps into walls forever: a flat, low plateau. The tall tower is the goal.
cap.2: Under all-left every non-terminal square is worth −0.04/(1 − 0.9) = −0.40. Height = 0.5 + value.
cap.3: V_π₀ ≡ −0.4 off the terminals: an endless −0.04 per step, discounted by γ = 0.9.

cap.1: One repaint: the square beside the goal now points at it, and its tower shoots up.
cap.2: After round 1 the square left of +1 points right; its value jumps to 0.96.
cap.3: Greedy improvement first changes the only state whose lookahead reaches the reward.

cap.1: Round by round, good news flows back from the goal, one square further each time.
cap.2: Each round connects one more ring of squares to the goal path, so their values rise in turn.
cap.3: Each evaluate-improve cycle propagates value one step further back along the path to the goal.

cap.1: Final round: every tower is as tall as it can get, and no sign wants repainting. The plan is the best one.
cap.2: At round 5 the policy is stable: V(start) = 0.49 and improvement changes nothing, so it is optimal.
cap.3: Stability means π is greedy w.r.t. its own V_π, which then satisfies the Bellman optimality equation.

predict.q: What does policy iteration alternate between?

options.t: Scoring the current plan, then greedily improving it

predict.why: Evaluate V_π, then set each state's action to the best one-step lookahead; repeat until stable.

predict.q: Your loop never stops: two policies keep swapping. Likely cause?

options.t: Ties in the argmax broken at random

predict.why: Equally good actions can flip each round. Break ties deterministically; np.argmax takes the first.

predict.q: When the policy stops changing, it is...
predict.why: A policy greedy with respect to its own values satisfies the Bellman optimality equation, so nothing beats it.

object.where: Any measure-then-adjust loop that ends when nothing changes: k-means, actor-critic training.
